sections.body_md:
An inequality can be active at a minimizer, or it can have room to spare. The two situations ask different things of the multiplier. Write each inequality as \(g_i(x) \le 0\). Stationarity still says that the objective gradient is balanced by a combination of the active constraint gradients. A constraint that is slack should not pull on that balance, so its multiplier is zero. A constraint that is active may pull, and the multiplier is then a weight on its gradient.

The sign of the weight is fixed by the inequality direction. With the residual written as \(g_i(x)\), the feasible side is the negative side, and the multiplier is nonnegative. A negative multiplier would push the stationarity equation the wrong way, toward the infeasible side. Complementary slackness is the bookkeeping that covers both situations at once: the product of the multiplier and the residual is zero. Either the residual is zero, or the multiplier is zero, or both.

Primal feasibility and dual feasibility are the remaining two lists. The point has to satisfy every constraint, and every inequality multiplier has to have the legal sign. Equality constraints, if any are present, keep free multipliers and stay in the stationarity equation. A point that fails any one of the four lists is not a KKT point, even if the other three lists are perfect.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(g(x) \le 0\),
\[

abla f(x) + J_g(x)^T 
u = 0, \quad g(x) \le 0, \quad 
u \ge 0, \quad 
u_i g_i(x) = 0.
\]
On an active bound \(x = b\) for \(\min (x - a)^2\), the multiplier is \(2(a - b)\) when the Lagrangian carries \(
u(x - b)\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \((t - 9)^2\) subject to \(t \le 4\). Stationarity is \(2(t - 9) + 
u = 0\). The branch \(
u = 0\) puts \(t\) at \(9\), and \(9 \le 4\) fails. The active branch puts \(t\) at \(4\).

The gate multiplier is 10. Stationarity gives \(2(4 - 9) + 
u = 0\), so \(
u = 10\), which is nonnegative. The objective is \(25\). Complementary slackness holds because the bound is active. The discarded branch was stationary and dual feasible and still illegal, because it was not primal feasible.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Accepting the inactive branch without checking the inequality is the standard miss. Stationarity and a zero multiplier are not enough. The point has to land inside the feasible set. A second miss is a positive multiplier on a strict inequality. The product is then nonzero. A third is a negative multiplier on an active bound. The sign is part of the system, not a free Lagrange multiplier. A fourth is to stop at the first case that is algebraically convenient. Both cases of the product have to be tried, and each survivor has to pass the lists it has not yet been checked against.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A linear program in standard form is an equality \(Ax = b\) plus the inequalities \(x \ge 0\). Its KKT system is stationarity of the Lagrangian, nonnegativity of both the primal variables and the dual slacks, and complementary products. Eliminating the primal variables leaves the dual linear program. The same four lists, applied to the squared distance to a half-space, produce the projection formula: stay put when the point is inside, and step along the normal when it is outside.
